title: A map, not a wall
hook: four pillars: what we believe, how we celebrate, how we live, how we pray

segments.voice: Yesterday, true self: holiness as becoming who you are before God. Your line was become who you are. Today, a new part of the path, and a big book.

On a shelf in a parish office sits a thick book. Not the Bible, the other one. Heavy, a little intimidating, full of numbered paragraphs. Sometimes there's one on a relative's nightstand with a rosary on top. From the outside it can look like a list of rules, a wall: everything you can't do. Open it, though, and it's built more like a map, with roads that connect. Today: the catechism.
screen: `THE OTHER BIG BOOK ON THE SHELF.` → `A LIST OF RULES?` → `BUILT MORE LIKE A MAP.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Catechism comes from a Greek verb, katechein, built on the word for sound, as in echo. It means to teach by word of mouth, to make something resound in someone's ear. Luke uses it at the start of his Gospel, telling a man named Theophilus he writes so that, in the Douay-Rheims, "thou mayest know the verity of those words in which thou hast been instructed." Instructed is that echo word. The faith was passed on out loud long before it was printed. Second, the book. There have been many catechisms. After the Council of Trent came the Roman Catechism in 1566. In the United States, the Baltimore Catechism of 1885 taught by question and answer: Why did God make you? To know him, to love him, and to serve him in this world, and to be happy with him forever in the next. In 1992, Pope John Paul II released the Catechism of the Catholic Church, the one on shelves today: two thousand eight hundred sixty-five numbered paragraphs. Third, the four pillars. It's built in four parts. What Catholics believe: the Creed. How they celebrate: the liturgy and the seven sacraments. How they live: life in Christ, the commandments and the virtues. And how they pray: ending with the Our Father. Belief, worship, life, prayer. Fourth, why a map. The Catechism isn't meant to be read cover to cover like a rulebook. It's meant to show how everything connects: why a belief shapes a sacrament, why a sacrament shapes a life, why a life turns into prayer. For the next weeks, this path walks it, one theme at a time.
screen: `KATECHEIN — TO MAKE IT ECHO.` · `TRENT, BALTIMORE, THEN 1992.` · `BELIEVE, CELEBRATE, LIVE, PRAY.` · `EVERYTHING CONNECTS.` · then, large: `FOUR PILLARS.`

segments.voice: Picture four stone columns holding up a roof, and touch each in turn: what you believe, or wonder about; how you celebrate, a Mass, a feast, a candle; how you live, one choice today; how you pray, or how you'd like to. Notice, with no judgment, which feels strongest in your life now and which feels thin. If you pray, ask for help with the thin one.
Catechism. From the Greek for making something echo: a summary of the faith, taught aloud and passed on. Today's Catechism has four pillars. Today's word.
Your line: four pillars. Believe, celebrate, live, pray. Day two hundred ninety, done.

howItsDone: Catholics use the Catechism of the Catholic Church as a reference for teaching the faith, and parishes build their classes for children, teens and adults joining the Church around its four parts.
